title: HTTP methods and Status Codes
summary: HTTP methods declare intent and status codes declare outcome. Get idempotency, safety, and the 2xx/4xx/5xx contract right and caches, retries, and clients behave without reading your body.

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: Methods are **intent**, status codes are **outcome**. Clients, proxies, caches, load balancers, and retry loops act on that pair *without reading your body*. If you return `200 OK` with `{"error": "not found"}` inside, you lied at the protocol layer and every layer above you will misbehave.

An HTTP interaction is a verb plus a result. The **method** (`GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`) tells the server and every intermediary what kind of operation the client wants and what guarantees to assume about safety and repeatability. The **status code** is a three-digit number where the first digit is the contract — `1xx` keep waiting, `2xx` it worked, `3xx` look elsewhere, `4xx` you sent garbage, `5xx` I failed on a valid request — and the next two digits narrow the reason. The reason phrase (`Not Found`, `Internal Server Error`) is for humans. The number is for machines. That distinction is the whole game in high-level design: you are designing a machine-readable contract, not a message.

For API design this means two separate promises. The method promises semantics: is this read-only, is repeating it safe, can a cache store it, can a retry replay it? The status promises responsibility: who must change behavior to make progress? `4xx` means resending the identical request is pointless — the client must fix auth, input, or addressing. `5xx` means the identical request may succeed later — the client should back off and retry. Conflate those and you get retry storms on bad input, poisoned caches, and clients that have to parse JSON to decide what happened. A clean API can be understood from method + path + status alone.

blocks.caption: The methods you will actually defend in a design review.
rows: Read one resource or list. No side effects. Cacheable by default.
Same as GET but headers only. Health checks, existence probes, size checks.
Discovery: CORS preflight, what methods this endpoint allows.
Create subordinate resource, trigger action, append. Server assigns identity.
Full replace at a client-chosen URL. Create-or-replace with same outcome on retry.
Partial update. Repeat may not be identical unless made conditional.
Remove resource. Second delete returns 404 or 204, state does not change further.

blocks.text: Two properties do all the heavy lifting: **safe** means no state change, so intermediaries can cache, prefetch, and replay it freely. **Idempotent** means repeating the request N times has the same server-side effect as doing it once, so it is retryable over an unreliable network. That is *why* `GET`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` are retry-friendly and `POST` is not. The trade-off is expressiveness versus safety: `POST` can do anything, which is exactly why caches ignore it and retry logic must treat it as dangerous. If you tunnel deletes through `POST /deleteUser` for convenience, you throw away idempotency signals, cache correctness, and automatic redirect handling. Choose the boring standard method. The ecosystem rewards you for it and punishes cleverness.
How a request becomes a status

blocks.title: From method to status
blocks.caption: Each hop acts on method + status, not the body.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  C[Client sends Method + Path + Headers] --> G[Gateway: rate limit, auth, routing]
  G --> S[Service: validate, authorize, execute]
  S --> O{Outcome}
  O -->|Success| OK[2xx + representation + cache directives]
  O -->|Moved| RD[3xx + Location header]
  O -->|Client fault| CE[4xx + machine-readable error code]
  O -->|Server fault| SE[5xx + Retry-After if transient]
  CE --> FIX[Client fixes request, no blind retry]
  SE --> RETRY[Client backs off and retries if idempotent]
  OK --> CACHE[Cache stores only safe methods]

blocks.text: The path through the system is deliberately layered. The edge — CDN, load balancer, gateway — enforces coarse policy before your code runs: is the caller over quota, is the token missing, is the route valid? Those become `429`, `401`, `404` without touching business logic. Your service then decides the finer split: validation failure is `400`, well-formed but semantically rejected is `422`, authenticated but forbidden is `403`, missing row is `404`, version conflict is `409` or `412`. Only if the request was valid and you failed anyway do you earn a `5xx`. The reason this layering matters is observability and control: edges can meter and shed `4xx` cheaply, while `5xx` must page someone. If your service returns `200` for every error, you blind every dashboard, autoscaler, and cache between you and the client.

blocks.caption: You need ~15 codes cold. Everything else is lookup.
rows: `200` read/update OK, `201` created + `Location`, `202` accepted async, `204` success with no body
`301` permanent move, `302/303` temporary + GET, `304` not modified, `307/308` preserve method
Fix the request, do not blind-retry
`400` bad syntax, `401` unauthenticated, `403` forbidden, `404` absent, `409` conflict, `422` semantic error, `429` throttled
`500` unexpected, `502` bad gateway, `503` unavailable + `Retry-After`, `504` gateway timeout
`100` continue large upload, `101` switch to websocket, `103` early hints for preload

blocks.text: Do not memorise 70 codes. Memorise the class contract plus the dozen that control client behavior differently. `201` versus `200` tells a client whether to follow `Location` to the new resource. `204` tells it there is deliberately no body to parse. `304` saves a full re-download. `401` triggers a token refresh, `403` does not — retrying a `403` with the same token is a loop. `404` versus `410` is intent: temporarily missing versus deliberately gone forever. `429` and `503` carry `Retry-After` and mean *back off*; `500` means *something broke, retry cautiously*. The specific number inside the class is an optimisation. Getting the first digit wrong is a correctness bug.
Trade-offs: why this design helps and hurts

blocks.caption: Every precise choice costs something.
rows: Clients branch without string-matching; caches and monitors work automatically
You must define and maintain a stable error schema and document every code per endpoint
One code path for naive clients; easy to prototype
Breaks caching, retries, CDNs, search indexing, and alerting. Every consumer hand-rolls logic. Do not do this.
PUT for create with client ID
Natural idempotency: retries safe, no duplicates
Client must generate unique IDs and handle create-vs-replace semantics
POST for create with server ID
Simple client, server owns identity and validation
Not idempotent by default; needs idempotency keys to allow safe retry
Correct retry, auth refresh, and cache eviction without docs-diving
More surface to get wrong; requires discipline in gateway vs service ownership

blocks.text: The classic failure is **lying with `200`**. A login failure returns `200` with `{"status": "fail"}`, a maintenance page returns `200` with HTML saying *down for maintenance*. The symptom you see: caches store the error for hours, uptime monitors report green while users cannot log in, and search engines index your outage text. The fix is blunt — error text with `200` is always wrong. The second failure is **auth confusion**: returning `403` when the token expired, or `401` when the user is simply not allowed. Symptom: mobile clients spin refreshing tokens forever on a `403`, or show a login screen for a permission problem that login will never fix. `401` means *who are you — authenticate*; `403` means *I know who you are — answer is no*. The third is **redirect and retry misuse**: a permanent move served as `302` keeps traffic and ranking on the dead URL forever, and a `POST` redirect via `301` gets silently rewritten to `GET` by old clients, dropping the body. Use `308` when method and body must survive. The fourth is **throttling without signals**: rejecting over-quota traffic with `403` or `500` instead of `429` plus `Retry-After`. Symptom: well-behaved SDKs cannot back off, so they hammer you harder and turn a quota event into an outage.

items: Symptom: cache serves stale error page → you returned `200` or `301` where `4xx/5xx/307` belonged, or forgot `Cache-Control: no-store` on errors.
Symptom: duplicate orders/users on retry → creation was `POST` with no idempotency key; should have been `PUT` or `POST` + `Idempotency-Key`.
Symptom: background jobs retry validation errors forever → you returned `500` for bad input; must be `400/422` so queues dead-letter instead of retrying.
Symptom: clients poll an async job with GET and get `200` with half-baked data → should be `202 Accepted` on submit, then `200` when done or `303` to result URL.
Symptom: large uploads fail after 30s of bytes → you skipped `100 Continue` / signed-URL pattern and force clients to send bodies you will reject.

blocks.text: Note what the code is buying. `201` plus `Location` means the client does not guess the new URL. `204` on delete means the client does not try to parse a body that is not there. `400` with a stable `type` field means the caller can branch programmatically instead of matching English text. The `Idempotency-Key` check is the trade-off made explicit: `POST` is convenient for server-assigned IDs, but you pay for safety by storing keys and returning the original result on replay. Without that, every timeout becomes a potential duplicate charge — the most expensive HTTP bug there is. Keep error shapes identical across endpoints. If `400` looks different on every route, consumers will ignore your precision and treat everything as generic failure.
How it shows up in an interview

items.title: Design a CRUD API for X
items.text: They expect resource naming, then method + status per operation: `POST → 201 + Location`, `GET → 200/404`, `PUT/PATCH → 200/404/409`, `DELETE → 204/404`. Say the code before they ask.

items.title: How does the client know to retry?
items.text: Answer with the class split: retry `502/503/504` and `429` with backoff and `Retry-After`; never retry `400/401/403/404/422`. Mention idempotency keys for `POST`.

items.title: How do you handle async work?
items.text: Return `202 Accepted` with a status URL, poll with `GET`, finish with `200` or redirect with `303 See Other`. Do not hold the connection open.

items.title: What about caching and versioning?
items.text: Tie `GET` safety to `ETag`/`304` and `Cache-Control`. Argue that version in URL vs header is secondary — status correctness matters more.

items.title: Walk a failure end to end
items.text: Pick expired token (`401` → refresh → replay), forbidden (`403` → stop), throttled (`429` → back off), deploy window (`503` → shed). Show you assign responsibility correctly.

items: `200` with an error body is simpler — it just pushes branching into every client, breaks intermediaries, and blinds monitoring. Simpler for you, harder for everyone else.

`401` and `403` are interchangeable — `401` means missing/bad authentication and should carry `WWW-Authenticate`; `403` means authenticated but not permitted. Clients refresh on the first and stop on the second.
`POST`, `PUT`, and `PATCH` are all updates — `PUT` is full replacement at a known URL, `PATCH` is a partial diff, `POST` is create-or-act. Using them randomly destroys retry safety.
`DELETE` returns `200` with the deleted object — prefer `204` with no body, or `200` only if you have a reason to return the tombstone. Pick one and be consistent.
`404` means the server is broken — no, `404` is a successful answer to a bad address. Reserve `5xx` for when a valid request failed on your side.
`301` and `308` are the same — `301/302` historically allow POST-to-GET rewriting; `307/308` preserve method and body. For API redirects that must keep `POST`, you want `307/308`.

blocks.text: When to use it and when not to

blocks.caption: Match the tool to the interaction, not habit.
rows: Bare `POST` with no replay protection on payments/orders
`PATCH` for full replace; semantics confuse retries
`PUT` with half an object — wipes fields you did not send
Blocking 60s request that times out through gateways
`403` or `200`-with-message that clients cannot back off on

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: Methods declare **intent and retryability**, status codes declare **outcome and responsibility** — `2xx` use it, `3xx` follow it, `4xx` fix the request, `5xx` back off and retry — and everything else is keeping that contract honest.
